clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic LAMA2 variants affecting the laminin alpha-2 chain (merosin) of laminin-211; it is the most common congenital muscular dystrophy in many Western populations.
Complete merosin deficiency presents in the neonatal period with profound hypotonia, weakness, poor antigravity movement and feeding and respiratory difficulty (the floppy infant).
Children with complete deficiency often achieve sitting but rarely walk independently, whereas partial deficiency causes a milder, later-onset, sometimes limb-girdle-like course.
A characteristic diffuse white-matter signal change on brain MRI becomes apparent after the early months of life and is usually accompanied by normal cognition.
Epilepsy affects a substantial minority despite the white-matter change, and occipital cortical malformation (such as polymicrogyria) is seen in some.
A demyelinating peripheral neuropathy is frequently present, since merosin is also expressed in the Schwann-cell basal lamina.
Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated, particularly in early disease.
Joint contractures, progressive scoliosis and respiratory insufficiency dominate long-term management.
reference.pathophysiology: LAMA2 encodes the laminin alpha-2 chain, which assembles with beta-1 and gamma-1 chains to form laminin-211 (merosin), the principal laminin of the skeletal-muscle basement membrane and a component of the peripheral-nerve basal lamina and cerebral vasculature. Laminin-211 bridges alpha-dystroglycan and the integrin alpha7-beta1 complex on the sarcolemma to the extracellular matrix, stabilising the fibre and transmitting contractile force. Absent or reduced merosin destabilises this linkage, causing sarcolemmal vulnerability, myofibre degeneration, impaired regeneration and fibrosis. The same deficiency in peripheral nerve produces dysmyelination, while an abnormal basement membrane at the blood-brain barrier underlies the characteristic cerebral white-matter change, which typically does not by itself impair cognition.
additionalDifferentials: Dystroglycanopathy-type congenital muscular dystrophies (Fukuyama, muscle-eye-brain disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome)
Collagen VI-related congenital muscular dystrophy (Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy)
Spinal muscular atrophy and other causes of the floppy infant
Leukodystrophies and other causes of infantile white-matter change when MRI is the presenting finding
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to demonstrate the white-matter signal change and to assess for cortical malformation
LAMA2 sequencing with deletion and duplication analysis, or a congenital muscular dystrophy gene panel
Muscle biopsy with laminin-alpha2 (merosin) immunostaining to distinguish complete from partial deficiency
Skin biopsy immunostaining for laminin-alpha2 as a less invasive alternative
Nerve conduction studies to detect the associated demyelinating neuropathy
Respiratory assessment including overnight studies, and a swallowing and feeding evaluation
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory distress or feeding failure with aspiration risk
Nocturnal hypoventilation as respiratory muscle strength and chest-wall compliance decline
Failure to thrive arising from feeding difficulty
reference.prognosis: Complete merosin deficiency causes severe, early-onset disability, with most children never walking and with substantial respiratory morbidity; survival depends heavily on respiratory and nutritional support. Partial deficiency is generally milder, with later onset and better motor attainment.
pitfalls: Interpreting the striking white-matter MRI change as a primary leukodystrophy and missing the underlying muscle disorder.
Assuming intellectual impairment from the MRI appearance, when cognition is usually normal.
Overlooking the associated demyelinating peripheral neuropathy.
Missing partial deficiency that presents later as a limb-girdle phenotype.
Deferring respiratory surveillance because the child is young and not yet overtly symptomatic.
management: Supportive, multidisciplinary care as no disease-modifying therapy currently exists
Proactive respiratory surveillance with non-invasive ventilation and cough-assist for hypoventilation and respiratory insufficiency
Nutritional and feeding support, including gastrostomy where feeding difficulty is severe
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and management of contractures, with surgical correction of scoliosis
Anticonvulsant therapy for epilepsy, which affects a substantial minority
Surveillance for cardiac involvement and the associated demyelinating neuropathy
Coordinated neuromuscular multidisciplinary team and genetic counselling for the family given autosomal recessive inheritance
